newsitem.title: ITALY: Commission backs move to allow Italian royals home.
newsitem.headline: Commission backs move to allow Italian royals home.

text.p: A government commission on Wednesday approved a move to allow Vittorio Emanuele, the son of Italy's last king, to return home from a 50-year exile from January 1, 1998, with full political rights.

Centre-left deputy Domenico Maselli told reporters the constitutional affairs commission of the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) voted for a constitutional draft to allow the return of the House of Savoy's male line.
The law would allow the royals to vote in the Italian republic, which threw out the monarchy in 1946 and forced Umberto II, Vittorio Emanuele's father, into exile in Portugal.
It consists of a simple phrase putting a time limit on the original ban on the monarchy having political rights and on the male line returning to Italy.
"The first two clauses of the current legislation will expire as of the first January 1998," it says.
"We are not putting limits on the civil right of the Savoys when they come back to Italy, as the government initially proposed," Maselli said.
But the commission did vote to keep a clause under which the republic took over confiscated property from the House of Savoy following their exile, he said.

Italian magazine Il Mondo said last month the royal family could stake a claim for the return of the property, including two castles, the Savoy villa and even the crown jewels, if they contested ownership in court.
The draft has to be approved by both houses of parliament twice in a complex process which could take several months.
The hard-left Communist Refoundation, on which Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left coalition relies for a majority, said it would oppose the measure.

"Communist Refoundation will fight with all its force against this constitutional modification which goes against the democratic and republican spirit," said its parliamentary leader, Oliviero Diliberto.

"The Savoys have never wanted to recognise our republic...They never recognised their responsability for the instalment of the fascist dictatorship...and for the shameful entry of Italy into the war on the side of the Nazis."

War-weary Italians voted to scrap the monarchy on June 2 1946, accusing their kings of complicity with more than 20 years of fascist rule under dictator Benito Mussolini, who led the country into World War Two in alliance with Nazi Germany.

The post-war republic decided to ban Umberto II and the male line of his family from ever returning to Italy. The family lived for a while in Portugal before moving to Switzerland, where Umberto died in 1983, leaving his son as heir.
Vittorio Emanuele, 59, caused outrage last month when he refused to apologise for fascist anti-semitic laws passed in 1938 when his grandfather, Vittorio Emanuele III, was king.
He has also said he will not renounce his royal prerogatives in order to smooth the passage of the bill.
